titleStmt.title: No. 906
The Israeli Ambassador (Eban) to the Secretary of State

div.head:
No. 906
The Israeli Ambassador (Eban) to the Secretary of State
div.p: Dear Mr. Secretary: The situation is so grave after our conversation today that I take the liberty of addressing my personal reflections to you even before consultation with my Government.

Our talk today was a most serious setback and disappointment. All the positive ideas which you expressed in your previous three
conversations have been completely excised from the document which you discussed with me this morning; and my only source of relief was to hear that the draft was as new to you as to me and does not commit your action or decision.

May I summarise the reasons which prompt me to describe this morning’s conversation as a sharp change for the worse in the situation which existed until then. On August 4 and August 7 I explained to you the facts and conditions which gave Israel its present sense of isolation and vulnerability. First, there is the implacable hostility of her neighbors; second, there is the enormous preponderance of the Arab States in relation to Israel in area, population and financial resources; third, there is the grave and extraordinary fact that all the security arrangements of the Western Powers in the Middle East have been directed and oriented towards the Arab States and have been based upon Israel’s exclusion. Arab States already possess binding defence treaties with Britain; they have been offered a mutual defence association with Turkey and Pakistan; the new Anglo-Egyptian treaty is directed exclusively to the reinforcement of the strongest Arab State and to the defence of other Arab States; and one American military aid agreement has been concluded with Iraq, while another one has been offered to Egypt.

The effect is a disturbance of the balance of strength and the enunciation of Israel’s exclusion as the guiding principle of security organization in the Middle East. In these circumstances our people have recently felt a growing alarm at the disadvantage in which they are being placed, as well as a profound sense of astonishment and disappointment at seeing the United States act in the Middle East with the effect of strengthening and encouraging Israel’s adversaries, while excluding Israel from any process of parallel reinforcement.

In response to this account you stated that you were impressed by the picture thus drawn of Israel’s sense of isolation and vulnerability; that in our situation you yourself would feel insecure and lonely; that if the effects of American policy were inadvertently to create disadvantage for Israel it would be your concern to cancel that disadvantage out; that you would like the Government and people of Israel to have a greater sense of security than they now possess; and that accordingly you would like us to consider whether it would be advantageous for the United States to formulate a Note to the Government of Israel.
Amongst the subjects to be included in such a Note you mentioned particularly:

list.item: (a) The resolve of the United States not to put Israel in a disadvantageous position;

(b) Israel’s eligibility for a military aid agreement with the United States. Here you stated that you did not exclude asking the Congress for a special provision in this respect; (I later pointed out that the existing legislation would make such eligibility possible);
(c) A more specific guarantee of Israel’s security than that contained in the 1950 Declaration; and
(d) Resolute efforts by the United States to bring about the unconditional cessation of the Suez Canal blockade restrictions.

div.p: You said that you were thinking of “something more than a restatement of generalities”.

After returning from Israel, where I found growing disquiet and concern at the current Western policy of making unilateral security arrangements with the Arab States, with Israel’s exclusion, I met you again on September 15. In that meeting I emphasised that the crux of the matter was the need to reassure Israel that the balance was not going to be substantively changed politically or practically in her disfavor.

If the United States Government would accept that principle there were two obvious corollaries. First, could not the United States formally convey to Israel that it was not the American intention to pursue military programs such as would effect a substantive change in the present balance; and second, should not the United States assert, as a matter of simple equality, that whatever military arrangements or relationships were to be offered to the Arab States, would be offered to Israel as well?
Having listened to my analysis you stated that you thought we could make some progress and should negotiate along the lines which you mentioned to me in August.

The news that you were approaching Israel’s security problems in a spirit of comprehension and sympathy had meanwhile spread amongst our people. It was a source of gratification and consolation. At the same time it was clear that if this moment were to be lost and to end in disillusionment, while the United States and Britain continued to base their security activities in the Middle East solely upon strengthening the Arab States and entering into agreements with them, then a situation of exceptional gravity would be created. Israel would conclude that her survival and security were in dire peril, and this sense of peril would inspire all her policies.

Against this background you will readily understand the disappointment which came upon me when I heard the terms of a draft which had been submitted to you this morning. That draft bears no relation to the lines of your own thought as you expressed them in previous conversations. There is no talk in the draft of a Note in
which the United States would seek to reassure Israel concerning her security. There is no mention of any intention to apply military policies in the Middle East in such a way as not to change the balance of power to Israel’s disadvantage. These is no talk of offering Israel inclusion in the military aid program, in which the two strongest Arab States have already been offered participation. There is no talk of any approach to a security guarantee for Israel which would go beyond the existing Declaration of May 1950.

In these circumstances, I must say that the draft submitted to you which I heard this morning would not merely fail to give us any sense of reassurance but would, I fear, have the reverse effect of confirming our worst fears and apprehensions; for the author of the draft does nothing to challenge the implication that the United States will pursue a policy of giving military aid agreements and arms to Arab States alone, while offering nothing politically or militarily to Israel.

I am writing this letter in the earnest hope that it may still be possible for action to be taken which would show respect for the vulnerability and insecurity of a small country whose hostile neighbors are being strengthened and encouraged by the security arrangements of the Western Powers. This would not be the only international occasion on which your personal statesmanship lifted a deadlock onto a new plane of hopeful progress. The feeling that this was to happen here moved me to attempt to persuade my Government and people that you understood our position and desired to alleviate it. You will, therefore, understand how grievously I was affected by hearing a draft which missed the whole spirit and content of your previous analysis. Only a deep concern for the historic relationship of our two countries would have impelled me, amidst your heavy preoccupations, to write to you as frankly as I have here. I hope that you will understand that I do so out of a sense of duty and in deep personal respect.
